mainTopic: Who pays when others contributed to the damage, and why the ניזק keeps the carcass and bears its drop in value
overview: The גמרא is looking for cases where other people helped cause damage, yet one person pays for all of it. Adding wood to a fire does not work as an example: either his liability is obvious, or he did nothing. רב פפא brings the ברייתא of a bench that breaks under a sixth person. After several tries, the גמרא explains it as a case where the bench broke the moment he leaned on the others, which teaches כחו כגופו דמי. The ten sticks case is left off the list, either because the list deals only with money or because the list would not follow a lone opinion against the רבנן. Next, the משנה's word 'תשלומי' teaches that the ניזק keeps the נבילה and the מזיק pays only the loss. Three פסוקים are brought as sources for this, and a צריכותא shows why each one is needed. רב כהנא asks why the תורה needs to give the carcass to the ניזק at all, and the answer is פחת נבילה, the carcass's drop in value. The amud ends by asking whether פחת נבילה is a dispute between תנאים, and that discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Adding wood to a fire is either obvious or meaningless
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tests the case of someone who adds wood to an existing fire. If the fire could not have spread without his wood, his liability is obvious. If it would have spread anyway, he did nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the fire would not have spread without him, then of course he is liable. But if it would have spread even without him, what did he actually do?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is checking whether the case of adding wood to a fire fits the rule being discussed. It shows that neither way of picturing the case works.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a two-sided trap. If his wood made the difference, he caused the whole damage himself, so it is פשיטא. If the fire would have spread anyway, he added nothing, so there is no reason to make him pay. Either way, this case does not teach the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: without him
it goes or spreads (here, the fire)
it is obvious, so there is no need to teach it
what did he do? He contributed nothing

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read this as saying the man is never liable. The point is only that this case can't be the new example the rule is meant to teach.

phrases.aramaic: אִי דִּבְלָאו אִיהוּ לָא אָזְלָא – פְּשִׁיטָא!
phrases.english: If without him it would not have spread, it is obvious!
Rather, if even without him it would have spread,
what did he do?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי דִּבְלָאו אִיהוּ לָא אָזְלָא – פְּשִׁיטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion about which case the rule comes to include
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion that the rule covers someone who adds wood to a fire
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Either the case is obvious, or the person caused nothing. Neither makes it a useful example.

steps.title: רב פפא brings the case of the broken bench
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא challenges the claim that the rule refers to only one case. He points to a ברייתא: five people sat on a bench without breaking it, a sixth sat and broke it, and the last one is liable. רב פפא adds that this means someone as heavy as פפא בר אבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא objected: There is also the ברייתא that says, if five people sat on one bench and did not break it, and one more came, sat on it, and broke it, the last one is liable. And רב פפא said this is a case like פפא בר אבא.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא challenges the גמרא by offering another case that seems to fit the rule: the last person to sit on a bench pays for breaking it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the first five people helped weaken the bench, yet the sixth person pays for everything. That looks exactly like 'adding to damage and being fully liable.' So רב פפא asks why this case was not listed as well.

keyTerms.meaning: he objected to it, a strong challenge
a bench
the last one is liable

phrases.english: Rav Pappa objected to it:
But there is also that which was taught:
Five who sat on one bench
and did not break it,
and one came and sat on it and broke it,
the last one is liable.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: כְּגוֹן פָּפָּא בַּר אַבָּא.
phrases.english: And Rav Pappa said: For example, Pappa bar Abba.
phrases.notes: He means someone very heavy, like פפא בר אבא.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לָהּ רַב פָּפָּא, וְהָא אִיכָּא הָא דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different case that might be what the rule includes
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the rule includes only one specific case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The bench case seems to be another example of someone finishing damage that others started and paying for all of it.

steps.title: The bench case is either obvious or meaningless too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא uses the same two-sided argument on the bench case. If the bench would not have broken without the sixth man, his liability is obvious. If it would have broken anyway, he did nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If you say the bench would not have broken without him, it is obvious. But if it would have broken even without him, what did he do?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away רב פפא's challenge by showing that the bench case has the same problem as the fire case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If his weight alone made the bench break, then he caused the damage, which is פשיטא. If the bench was going to break anyway, he caused nothing. So the bench case can't be the example the rule is teaching either.

keyTerms.meaning: what is the case? How do we picture it?
if you say
it would break

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?

phrases.aramaic: אִילֵּימָא דִּבְלָאו אִיהוּ לָא אִיתְּבַר – פְּשִׁיטָא.
phrases.english: If you say that without him it would not have broken, it is obvious.
Rather, if even without him it would also have broken,
what did he do?

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָמֵי? אִילֵּימָא דִּבְלָאו אִיהוּ לָא אִיתְּבַר – פְּשִׁיטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב פפא's challenge using the same reasoning as step 1
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the bench case as a proof that the rule includes more cases
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The bench case is either obvious or shows no contribution by the last person, just like the fire case.

steps.title: So how do we explain the bench ברייתא?
steps.stepSummary: After pushing the bench case aside, the גמרא is left with a problem. The ברייתא itself still needs an explanation, since both ways of reading it seemed to fail.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the end, how is the ברייתא to be explained?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how the bench ברייתא can make sense at all. This sets up the next move, where an answer will be given.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two-sided argument did more than reject רב פפא's challenge. It also seemed to leave the ברייתא with no sensible meaning: either it teaches something obvious, or it makes someone pay who did nothing. So the ברייתא now needs its own explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: in the end, after all
a taught source; here, the ברייתא
is it explained or resolved

phrases.english: Ultimately, how is the teaching to be explained?
phrases.notes: Here מתניתא means the ברייתא about the bench, not our משנה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Points out that the rejection in step 3 leaves the bench ברייתא unexplained
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A workable reading of the bench ברייתא that is neither obvious nor about someone who contributed nothing

steps.title: The bench would have broken later, but he made it break sooner
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the ברייתא as a case where the bench would have broken in two hours anyway, but the sixth man made it break in one hour. The first five can tell him that without him they would have gotten up in time.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the ברייתא is needed for a case where, without him, the bench would have broken in two hours, and now it broke in one hour. The first five can say to him: "If not for you, we would have sat a little longer and then stood up."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the problem from Step 4 by finding a middle case between the two sides it rejected.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, there were only two options: the bench would never have broken, or it would have broken right away anyway. Now there is a third option: it would have broken eventually, but the sixth man sped it up. So the first five can claim they would have stood up before the two hours ended, which means only he caused the damage.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not needed (except for this case). It introduces the specific case where a teaching is needed.
In two hours
In one hour
A little bit more

phrases.english: No, it is needed

phrases.aramaic: דִּבְלָאו אִיהוּ הָוֵי מִיתְּבַר בִּתְרֵי שָׁעֵי,
phrases.english: where without him it would have broken in two hours,
phrases.notes: "Him" is the sixth man, the last one who sat down.

phrases.english: and now it broke in one hour;
because they can say to him:

phrases.aramaic: אִי לָאו אַתְּ – הָוֵי יָתְבִינַן טְפֵי פּוּרְתָּא,
phrases.english: Were it not for you, we would have sat a little longer,
and stood up.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא; דִּבְלָאו אִיהוּ הָוֵי מִיתְּבַר בִּתְרֵי שָׁעֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the open question from Step 4 by offering a new case for the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines a narrower case: the damage was sped up, not newly caused.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא could not be explained, because either the sixth man obviously caused the break or he did nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is talking about speeding up a break that would have happened later, so the first five are free and he alone pays.

steps.title: The sixth man can blame the first five
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: the sixth man can answer back that the bench would not have broken under his weight alone, so the five share the blame.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let him say to them: "If not for you, it would not have broken under me alone!"
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from Step 5 by giving the sixth man a strong reply to the first five.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first five said, "Without you, we would have stood up in time." But he can say just as easily, "Without you, my weight alone would never break it." Since both sides helped cause the break, there is no reason he alone should pay.

keyTerms.meaning: But let him say to them
With mine alone (under my weight)

phrases.english: But let him say to them:
Were it not for you,
under mine alone it would not have broken!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the case suggested in Step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the first five are free because they would have stood up in time.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The sixth man has an equal counterclaim: his weight alone would not break the bench, so everyone shares the cause and he should not pay alone.

steps.title: It broke the moment he leaned on them
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers a new case: the bench broke at the very moment the sixth man leaned on the others.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a case where, as he leaned on them, it broke.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a new case for the ברייתא, one where the sixth man has no reply to the others.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the bench broke right away when he leaned on them, the first five had no chance to stand up and could not have stopped anything. So his reply "without you it would not have broken" no longer works, because the five were helpless.

keyTerms.meaning: At the same time as, while
Leans on

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where as he leaned on them, it broke.
phrases.notes: "Them" means the five people already sitting on the bench.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּבַהֲדֵי דְּסָמֵיךְ בְּהוּ, תְּבַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 6 by changing the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changes the case so the first five could not have prevented the damage.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The bench broke over time, so the sixth man could blame the five.
steps.terutzMaskana: The bench broke instantly as he leaned on them, so he alone caused it.

steps.title: Then the ruling is obvious
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that in this new case it is obvious the sixth man alone pays, so why would the ברייתא need to teach it?
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on Step 7: if he broke the bench instantly, his liability needs no teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ברייתא is supposed to teach something new. If the sixth man broke the bench the moment he leaned on helpless people, of course only he pays, so the new case seems to make the ברייתא pointless again.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious. Used to ask why a source bothers to teach something so clear.

steps.confusionAlert: Here פשיטא is not a final ruling. It is a challenge: the גמרא is saying the answer is too obvious to be what the ברייתא means.

phrases.english: It is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the case suggested in Step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation that the bench broke instantly when the sixth man leaned on the others.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In that case his sole liability is obvious, so the ברייתא would be teaching nothing new.

steps.title: Force counts like body
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is needed to teach that damage done by one's force (כחו) is treated like damage done by one's body (גופו).
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have thought that a person's force is not like his body. So the ברייתא teaches that his force is like his body: wherever he would be liable for breaking something with his body, he is also liable for breaking it with his force.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 8 (why the ברייתא needed to teach the bench case). The sixth man broke the bench by leaning on the others, so it was his force, not his body, that broke it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the sixth man only leaned on the other five, you might think their weight shares the blame and that he did not break it 'himself'. The ברייתא teaches that כחו כגופו דמי: pushing through others counts as if his own body broke the bench, so he alone pays.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said / I would have thought (introduces a mistaken idea)
His force: damage caused by his push or pressure, not by direct body contact
His body: damage caused directly by his own body
It teaches us (the new point the source is coming to make)

steps.whatToRemember: The bench case teaches כחו כגופו דמי: breaking something by pressing through others counts as if you broke it with your own body.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule that a person's direct force is like his body comes up again and again in the laws of damages.

phrases.english: You might have said
his force is not like his body
phrases.notes: He leaned on the other men instead of sitting on the bench himself, so it was only his push that broke it.

phrases.aramaic: קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן דְּכֹחוֹ כְּגוּפוֹ דָּמֵי,
phrases.english: so it teaches us that his force is like his body
that anywhere that his body breaks something (he is liable)
when his force breaks it, it is also considered breaking (and he is liable)

steps.triggerLanguage: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא, כֹּחוֹ לָאו כְּגוּפוֹ דָּמֵי; קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 8's question of why the ברייתא needs to teach something that seems obvious.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifies a hidden חידוש (new teaching) in a case that looked obvious
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the sixth man only leaned on others, his force is not like his body, so the five should share the liability.
steps.terutzMaskana: כחו כגופו דמי: he alone is liable, just as if his body broke the bench.

steps.title: Why is the ten sticks case missing?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא's list leaves out the case of ten people who beat a man to death, where רבי יהודה בן בתירא makes the last one liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are there no more cases? But there is the ברייתא: If ten people hit a man with ten sticks, whether all at once or one after the other, and he died, they are all exempt. רבי יהודה בן בתירא says: If they hit him one after the other, the last one is liable, because he brought his death closer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the list of cases in the ברייתא by pointing to another case that seems to fit the same idea: many people helped, but the last one is responsible.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא's list is made of cases where others contributed, yet one person carries the full liability. According to רבי יהודה בן בתירא, the last hitter is liable even though the first nine also hurt the man, which looks just like the bench case. So why didn't the ברייתא include it?

keyTerms.meaning: And is there no more? (asks why a list is missing a case)
Sticks
All at once, at the same moment
One after the other
He brought his death closer, made him die sooner

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up רבי יהודה בן בתירא with רבי (רבי יהודה הנשיא), who comes up later in this section. They are two different people.

phrases.english: And are there no more cases?
phrases.notes: He means more cases for the list of 'others helped, but one person pays it all'.

phrases.english: But there is that which is taught in a ברייתא:

phrases.aramaic: הִכּוּהוּ עֲשָׂרָה בְּנֵי אָדָם בְּעֶשֶׂר מַקְלוֹת,
phrases.english: If ten people hit him with ten sticks,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין בְּבַת אַחַת בֵּין בָּזֶה אַחַר זֶה,
phrases.english: whether all at once or one after the other,
and he died, they are all exempt.
רבי יהודה בן בתירא says:
If they hit him one after the other, the last one is liable,
because he brought his death closer!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתוּ לֵיכָּא? וְהָא אִיכָּא הָא דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: With the bench case settled, the גמרא asks why another similar case is missing from the ברייתא's list.
steps.kashyaTarget: The completeness of the ברייתא's list of cases
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ten sticks case (according to רבי יהודה בן בתירא) fits the same pattern, so the ברייתא should have listed it.

steps.title: The list does not deal with the death penalty
steps.stepSummary: First answer: the ברייתא only deals with paying for damage, not with the death penalty.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not talking about killing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a first answer to step 10: the ten sticks case is about a death penalty, and the ברייתא's list is only about money damages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ten sticks case is about whether someone is put to death for murder. The ברייתא lists only cases of paying for damage, so a case about the death penalty was never meant to be on that list.

keyTerms.meaning: Killing; here, liability for the death penalty
It is speaking about, it deals with
Not

phrases.english: It is not speaking about (liability for) killing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 10 by limiting the ברייתא's subject.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the scope of the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ten sticks case belongs on the list.
steps.terutzMaskana: The list covers only damages, so death penalty cases are not included.

steps.title: The list leaves out disputed cases
steps.stepSummary: Second answer: the ברייתא does not bring cases that are in dispute, and the ten sticks case is a dispute.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: it is not speaking about a case that is in dispute.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second, different answer to step 10. The ten sticks case is a מחלוקת, and the ברייתא only lists cases that are not argued about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ten sticks case, the תנא קמא exempts everyone and only רבי יהודה בן בתירא makes the last one liable. Since the case is a פלוגתא, the ברייתא would not use it as an example.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (introduces a second answer)
A dispute, a case the חכמים argue about

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
it is not speaking about a case that is in dispute.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, separate answer to the same question from step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the scope of the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ten sticks case belongs on the list.
steps.terutzMaskana: The list does not include cases that are in dispute.

steps.title: But the list already has a disputed case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the second answer: an earlier case in the list was already explained as following the רבנן against רבי, so the list does include a dispute.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it doesn't? But we already explained that it is not like רבי!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from step 12. We already said an earlier case on the list follows one side of a מחלוקת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the גמרא explained a case on this same list (the pit case) as following the רבנן and not רבי. That means the ברייתא does bring disputed cases. So 'it doesn't speak about disputes' cannot be true.

keyTerms.meaning: And it doesn't?! (a surprised challenge)
We established, we explained it as

phrases.english: And it doesn't (speak about disputes)?!
But we explained it as not following רבי!
phrases.notes: This points back to the pit case earlier on the list, which we explained as following the רבנן, not רבי.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the second answer given in step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the ברייתא does not bring disputed cases
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An earlier case on the same list was already explained as following one side of a dispute (the רבנן against רבי).

steps.title: Following the majority is different
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא may follow the majority (רבנן) against one Sage, but it would not follow a single Sage (רבי יהודה בן בתירא) against the majority.
steps.simpleTranslation: We explain it as not like רבי and like the רבנן. But we do not explain it as like רבי יהודה בן בתירא and not like the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the second answer by making it more exact. The rule is not 'no disputes at all' but 'no cases that go against the רבנן'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the pit case, the ברייתא follows the רבנן, the majority, so it is fine to include. The ten sticks case is liable only according to רבי יהודה בן בתירא, a single opinion against the רבנן, so the ברייתא would not list it. The second answer from step 12 stands.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis, the majority of the חכמים
We explain it as, we set it up as following

steps.whatToRemember: The ten sticks case is missing from the list either because the list deals only with money damages, or because the ברייתא would not follow a lone opinion against the רבנן.

phrases.english: Not like רבי and like the רבנן, we do explain it;

phrases.aramaic: כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתֵירָא – וְלָא כְּרַבָּנַן,
phrases.english: like רבי יהודה בן בתירא and not like the רבנן,
we do not explain it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 13 and saves the second answer from step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Makes the earlier rule more exact
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the list includes one disputed case, it should include any disputed case.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא may follow the majority in a dispute, but it would not follow a lone opinion against the רבנן.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The ten sticks case is left off because the ruling that the last one is liable comes only from רבי יהודה בן בתירא, against the רבנן.

steps.title: The extra word 'payments' teaches that the owner keeps the carcass
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that the משנה says 'תשלומי נזקו' instead of 'נזקו.' This wording teaches the ברייתא's law that the owner deals with the נבילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'I am liable for the payments of its damage.' It does not say 'I am liable for its damage.' It says 'for the payments of its damage.' So the משנה already teaches what the רבנן taught in a ברייתא: 'Payments of damage' teaches that the owners deal with the carcass.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new phrase from the משנה and points out a careful choice of words. It shows that this wording teaches a known law from a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word תשלומין is related to the word for 'complete.' So the damager does not pay the full value of the animal. The owner keeps the dead animal (and its value), and the damager just pays the difference to complete the loss.

keyTerms.meaning: Payments for damage; here, paying only to make up the loss
It does not teach / it does not say
Deal with the carcass: the owner keeps it and carries its loss in value
An animal that died without proper שחיטה; a carcass

steps.confusionAlert: 'The owners deal with the carcass' does not mean the owner just has to clean it up. It means the carcass stays his, so the damager pays only the difference between the live animal and the carcass.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the basic way damages are paid: the damager pays the loss in value, and the injured party keeps whatever is left.

phrases.english: I am liable for the payments of its damage.
It does not say: 'I am liable for its damage,'
rather: 'for the payments of its damage.'
So we have learned what the Rabbis taught:
'Payments of damage' —
teaches that the owners deal with the carcass.
phrases.notes: The owner keeps the dead animal and takes its lower value; the damager pays only the difference.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the discussion of the ברייתא's list (steps 10-14) and starts a new phrase of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's word 'תשלומי' teaches that the owner keeps the carcass and the damager pays only the loss in value, which is the same as the ברייתא.

steps.title: Where do we learn this law from?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source in the תורה for the rule that the owner keeps the carcass.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where are these things learned?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a פסוק that teaches the law it just learned. This is a setup line: the next two steps give two different answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה and ברייתא state the law, but the גמרא wants to know its root in the תורה. This is a request for information, not an attack.

keyTerms.meaning: From where are these things learned? (asking for a source)

phrases.english: From where are these matters learned?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the law stated in step 15.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A פסוק that teaches that the damager only completes the loss and the owner keeps the carcass.

steps.title: רבי אמי: read 'he shall complete it' instead of 'he shall pay it'
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי learns it from the פסוק 'מכה נפש בהמה ישלמנה' by reading ישלמנה as ישלימנה, 'he shall complete it.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אמי said: The פסוק says, 'One who strikes an animal shall pay for it (ישלמנה).' Do not read it 'ישלמנה' (he shall pay for it), but 'ישלימנה' (he shall complete it).
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי gives the first source. He reads one word of the פסוק with different vowels so it means 'complete' instead of 'pay.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Complete it' means the damager only fills in what is missing. The carcass already covers part of the value, so he pays just the rest.

keyTerms.meaning: As the פסוק says
Do not read (the word this way, but read it another way)
He shall complete it

phrases.english: Rabbi Ami said: As the verse says:
'One who strikes an animal shall pay for it' —
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:18

phrases.english: do not read it 'he shall pay for it,'
but rather 'he shall complete it.'
phrases.notes: Same letters, different vowels, so the meaning shifts from paying to filling in what's missing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The source is ויקרא 24:18, read as 'ישלימנה' (he shall complete it), teaching that the damager only completes the loss.

steps.title: רב כהנא: 'he pays up to the torn animal' from the פסוק of the שומר
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא learns the same law from 'הטרפה לא ישלם': he pays up to the value of the torn animal, but not for the torn animal itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: We learn it from here: 'If it was torn by a wild animal, let him bring a witness; the torn animal he shall not pay.' Read it as: 'He pays up to the torn animal,' but the torn animal itself he does not pay for.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא gives a second, different source for the same law. He reads the פסוק about a torn animal to mean that the payer covers only the loss, not the remaining torn animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He reads the word עֵד (witness) as עַד (until). So the payer pays 'until' the value of the torn animal, the gap between healthy and torn. The torn animal itself stays with the owner, just like the carcass in the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: From here (a different source)
An animal torn by a wild beast
Until / up to
Itself

steps.whatToRemember: The damager pays only the difference in value. The owner keeps the carcass or torn animal. רבי אמי learns this from 'ישלימנה' (complete it), and רב כהנא from 'עד טרפה ישלם' (pay up to the torn animal).

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said: From here:
'If it was torn to pieces, let him bring it as a witness,'
phrases.notes: שמות 22:12

phrases.english: 'the torn animal he shall not pay' —
read it: 'up to the torn animal he shall pay,'
phrases.notes: He reads the word עֵד ('witness') as if it said עַד ('until') and joins it to the next words.

phrases.english: but the torn animal itself he shall not pay for.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, different answer to the question of step 16, next to רבי אמי's answer.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The source is שמות 22:12, read as 'עד טרפה ישלם': the payer covers the loss up to the torn animal's value, and the torn animal itself stays with the owner.

steps.title: חזקיה's source: the dead animal belongs to the damaged party
steps.stepSummary: חזקיה gives a third source. 'וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לּוֹ' means the carcass goes to the ניזק.
steps.simpleTranslation: חזקיה said: we learn it from here: 'And the dead one shall be his', meaning it belongs to the damaged party.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is still answering the question from Step 16: where does the תורה teach that the owner keeps the carcass? חזקיה gives a third answer, from a different פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אמי and רב כהנא each read a word closely ('ישלמנה' and 'הטרפה לא ישלם'). חזקיה uses a פסוק that says outright that the dead animal is 'his'. He reads 'his' as the ניזק's.

keyTerms.meaning: From here, meaning 'this is my source'
'And the dead one shall be his' (שמות כא:לו)
The damaged party, whose ox was killed

phrases.english: Ḥizkiyya said: from here:
"And the dead one shall be his": to the injured party.
phrases.notes: שמות כא:לו. The פסוק just says 'his'. חזקיה is telling us whose: the ניזק's.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third source for the same rule, alongside רבי אמי (Step 17) and רב כהנא (Step 18)
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source in the תורה for the rule that the ניזק keeps the carcass (from Step 16)
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לּוֹ', read as 'to the ניזק'

steps.title: A ברייתא from חזקיה's school says the same thing
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא taught in the school of חזקיה reads 'לו' as the ניזק. It raises the idea that it could mean the מזיק, and rejects it with the words 'לא כך היה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so it was taught in the school of חזקיה: 'And the dead one shall be his' means the damaged party. Do you say it means the damaged party, or maybe only the one who did the damage? You should say: it could not have been that.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that backs up חזקיה's reading. The ברייתא asks whether 'his' could mean the person who caused the damage, and rejects that very briefly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'לו' could point to either person, so the ברייתא has to rule one of them out. It rejects the מזיק reading with just 'לא כך היה' and gives no reason. That gap sets up the גמרא's next question.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in the school of חזקיה (a ברייתא)
The one who caused the damage, the owner of the goring ox
'Do you say... or is it only...': a way of testing another possible reading
'It could not have been that': a short rejection

steps.confusionAlert: 'לו' (his) on its own does not tell you whose. The whole discussion is about whether it means the ניזק or the מזיק. The conclusion is the ניזק.

phrases.english: And so it was taught in the school of Ḥizkiyya:
"And the dead one shall be his": to the injured party.
Do you say it means the injured party,
or is it perhaps only the one who did the damage?
You should say: it could not have been that.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up חזקיה's reading (Step 19) with a ברייתא from his own school
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of the school of חזקיה

steps.title: What does 'it could not have been that' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the ברייתא means by its short rejection, 'לא כך היה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'it could not have been that' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to ask about the ברייתא's unclear words. It is setting up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא rejected the מזיק reading but gave no reason. The גמרא wants to know the logic behind that rejection.

keyTerms.meaning: What, meaning 'what does it mean?'

phrases.english: What does "it could not have been that" mean?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the ברייתא's rejection in Step 20

steps.title: אביי: the extra words of the פסוק show the carcass goes to the damaged party
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains: if the carcass belonged to the מזיק, the תורה could have stopped at 'שור תחת השור'. The extra words 'והמת יהיה לו' must be teaching that it goes to the ניזק.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: if you thought the carcass belonged to the one who did the damage, the תורה should have written 'an ox for the ox' and stopped. Why do I need 'and the dead one shall be his'? Learn from this that it belongs to the damaged party.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question from Step 21. He shows that reading 'his' as the מזיק would make the end of the פסוק unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the מזיק pays a whole new ox, it would be obvious that the dead ox becomes his. The תורה would not need to say so. Since the תורה did add 'והמת יהיה לו', those words must teach something new: the carcass stays with the ניזק.

keyTerms.meaning: If it enters your mind, meaning 'if you thought that'
The Merciful One, a name for the תורה or ה׳
And let it be silent, meaning stop and say no more
Why do I need it? Used when words seem extra
Learn from it: the conclusion

steps.whatToRemember: There are three sources for the rule that the ניזק keeps the carcass: רבי אמי ('ישלמנה'), רב כהנא ('הטרפה לא ישלם'), and חזקיה ('והמת יהיה לו'). אביי explains חזקיה's source: if the carcass went to the מזיק, those words would be unnecessary.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common way the גמרא learns from a פסוק. If the words would add nothing under one reading, the תורה must mean the other reading.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
If it enters your mind
that the carcass belongs to the one who did the damage,
let the Merciful One write "an ox for the ox,"
phrases.notes: שמות כא:לו. This is the part of the same פסוק just before 'והמת יהיה לו'.

phrases.english: and be silent;
why do I need "and the dead one shall be his"?
Learn from it: it belongs to the injured party.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: אִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ נְבֵילָה דְּמַזִּיק הָוְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 21 by explaining the ברייתא's reasoning
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why reading 'לו' as the מזיק is impossible
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Under the מזיק reading, 'והמת יהיה לו' would be unnecessary, since 'שור תחת השור' would be enough. So the words must mean the ניזק.

steps.title: Why 'one who strikes an animal' alone is not enough
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins a צריכותא. If the תורה had written only 'מכה בהמה ישלמנה', we might think the rule applies only there, because striking an animal is uncommon. A טרפה is common, so we might think the full rule does not apply to it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And all the sources are needed. Suppose the תורה had written only 'one who strikes an animal shall pay for it.' I would say the rule applies there because it does not happen often. But a torn animal is common, so I would say the rule does not apply. That is why we need the other source too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers an unspoken question: why do we need three sources for the same law? It starts by showing that the first source could not teach the case of a טרפה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difference here is how often each case happens. A person hitting someone's animal is rare, so the תורה might go easy on him. Animals being torn happens all the time, so we might have thought the full value must be paid there.

keyTerms.meaning: It is necessary. This word opens a list of reasons why each source is needed.
The Merciful One, meaning the תורה
Common, something that happens often
An animal fatally torn or injured

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not doubting the law itself. It is only explaining why the תורה wrote it in more than one place.

phrases.english: And it is necessary, for if the Merciful One had written only
"One who strikes an animal shall pay for it"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:21

phrases.english: I would say the rule applies there because it is uncommon
but a torn animal, which is common
I would say the rule does not apply; so the other source is necessary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After three sources were given for one law, the גמרא explains why each one is needed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Unspoken question: why are three sources needed for one law?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The source about striking an animal is limited because that case is uncommon. It cannot teach the common case of a טרפה.

steps.title: Why the torn-animal source alone is not enough
steps.stepSummary: If the תורה had taught only the case of the טרפה, we might think the rule applies only there, because the damage happened by itself. A person who strikes an animal does it with his own hands, so we might think the full value must be paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the תורה had taught us only the torn animal, I would say the rule applies there because the damage happened by itself. But one who strikes an animal does it with his own hands, so I would say the rule does not apply.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא flips the direction. Now it shows that the טרפה source could not teach the case of a person striking an animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difference now is direct versus indirect damage. With a טרפה, the person did not do the damage himself. With someone who strikes an animal, he acted with his own hands, so we might have been stricter with him.

keyTerms.meaning: It taught us
By itself. The person did not cause the damage directly.
With one's own hands, direct action

phrases.english: And if it had taught us only the torn animal
I would say the rule applies there because it happened by itself
but one who strikes an animal, which is done with his own hands
I would say the rule does not apply.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The reverse side of step 23. Each of the first two sources cannot teach the other.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The טרפה source is limited because that damage happened by itself. It cannot teach the case of direct striking.

steps.title: Why the first two sources still cannot teach the goring ox
steps.stepSummary: Even with both sources, each has its own easy-going feature. Striking is uncommon, and a טרפה happens by itself. An ox goring is both common and counts as direct, so we would still need 'והמת יהיה לו'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the תורה had taught us only these two, I would say: this one has the rule because it is uncommon, and that one because it happened by itself. But 'and the dead one shall be his' is a case that is common and counts as by hand, so I would say the rule does not apply.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now explains why we need the third source, 'והמת יהיה לו'. The first two sources together still could not teach it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each of the first two cases had a 'softening' feature. The goring-ox case has neither one: it is common and it counts as direct. So we could not learn it from them, even by combining both.

keyTerms.meaning: These two, meaning the first two sources
And the dead one shall be his. This is the source about the ox goring an ox.

phrases.english: And if it had taught us only these two
I would say this one has the rule because it is uncommon
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the person who strikes an animal.

phrases.english: and that one because it happened by itself
phrases.notes: 'That one' is the torn animal.

phrases.english: but "and the dead one shall be his"
phrases.notes: שמות 21:36, about one ox goring another.

phrases.english: which is common and counts as by hand
phrases.notes: The ox did the goring, but here it counts like the owner's own action, since he was supposed to guard it.

phrases.english: I would say the rule does not apply.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After showing the first two sources need each other, the גמרא shows they still cannot teach the third case.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The goring-ox case is common and counts as direct. Neither softening feature applies, so it needs its own source.

steps.title: Why the goring-ox source alone is not enough, so all three are needed
steps.stepSummary: If the תורה had written only 'והמת יהיה לו', we might think the rule applies only when a person's property does the damage. A person who strikes an animal damages with his own body, so we might think the full value must be paid. Therefore all the sources are necessary.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the תורה had taught us only 'and the dead one shall be his,' I would say the rule applies there because it is his property that does the damage. But here, where he damages with his own body, I would say the rule does not apply. So all the sources are necessary.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the צריכותא. It shows that the goring-ox source could not teach the case of a person striking an animal, so every source is needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new difference is property versus body. When your ox damages, it is your property acting, which is a lighter case. When you damage with your own body, we might have thought you must pay in full. So the source about striking an animal is still needed.

keyTerms.meaning: Property, here the person's ox
With his own body
Causes damage. Also the name for the one who caused it.

steps.whatToRemember: All three sources teach the same law: the carcass stays with the ניזק, and the מזיק pays only the loss. Each source is needed because each case has a feature that could have limited the rule. Striking an animal is uncommon. A טרפה happens by itself. A goring ox is property, not the person's body.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a classic צריכותא. The גמרא shows that no verse in the תורה is extra, even when several verses seem to teach the same thing.

phrases.english: And if it had taught us only "the dead one shall be his"
I would say the rule applies there because it is his property that does the damage
but here, where he does the damage with his own body
phrases.notes: 'Here' is the person who strikes someone's animal.

phrases.english: I would say the rule does not apply; so it is necessary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the צריכותא. The third source cannot teach the first, so all three are needed.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Each of the three sources is needed, because each case has a feature that could have limited the rule to that case alone.

steps.title: רב כהנא restates the assumption
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא spells out the assumption behind the earlier derivation: without 'והמת יהיה לו', the carcass would have belonged to the מזיק.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said to רב: So the only reason the carcass goes to the ניזק is that the תורה wrote 'והמת יהיה לו'. Without it, would I have said the carcass belongs to the מזיק?
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא is setting up a challenge. First he states clearly what the earlier explanation assumes, so he can attack it in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 22 said the extra words 'והמת יהיה לו' teach that the carcass goes to the ניזק. That only works if, without those words, we would have given the carcass to the מזיק. רב כהנא puts that assumption on the table so he can test whether it matters at all.

keyTerms.meaning: The carcass of the dead animal
The one responsible for the damage
I would have thought

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said to Rav:
But the reason is that the Merciful One wrote
"And the dead one shall be his,"
phrases.notes: שמות 21:36

phrases.english: but if not for that, I would have said:
the carcass belongs to the damager?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns back to the derivation from 'והמת יהיה לו' in Step 22 and spells out its hidden assumption
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is it really true that without the פסוק the carcass would belong to the מזיק?

steps.title: The damager could pay with the carcass anyway
steps.stepSummary: Any item worth money, even bran, counts as payment. So even if the carcass were the מזיק's, he could pay with it. Why would the תורה need to give it to the ניזק?
steps.simpleTranslation: Now, if the מזיק had several carcasses of torn animals, he could give them as payment, as the Master said: 'ישיב' includes anything worth money, even bran. Do we even need a פסוק to say he can pay with this carcass, which is the ניזק's own animal?
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא challenges the need for the פסוק. Even if the carcass belonged to the מזיק, the end result would be the same.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since 'ישיב' allows payment with any item worth money, the מזיק could pay with the carcass of any animal. He could surely pay with the carcass of the ניזק's own animal. So giving the carcass to the ניזק seems to change nothing, and the פסוק seems pointless.

keyTerms.meaning: Here, carcasses of animals that were torn and died
'He shall pay back', the source that payment can be in goods
Anything worth money
Bran, a cheap grain product

phrases.english: Now, if he himself had
several torn carcasses, he could give them to him,
phrases.notes: 'He' is the מזיק, and 'him' is the ניזק, who would get the carcasses as payment.

phrases.english: as the Master said: "He shall pay back"
comes to include anything worth money,
and even bran;
is it necessary to say his own?!
phrases.notes: 'His own' means the ניזק's own dead animal. If he can pay with anyone's carcass, surely he can pay with this one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the assumption laid out in Step 27 to argue that the פסוק adds nothing
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that 'והמת יהיה לו' is needed to give the carcass to the ניזק
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Since 'ישיב' allows payment with any item of value, the practical result is the same whoever owns the carcass, so the פסוק seems unnecessary

steps.title: The verse is needed for the carcass's drop in value
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק matters for פחת נבילה. If the carcass loses value before the case comes to בית דין, the ניזק bears that loss.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed only for the drop in value of the carcass.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רב כהנא. Who owns the carcass does make a practical difference: who loses out when the carcass becomes worth less over time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the carcass were the מזיק's, any drop in its value before payment would be his loss. Because the תורה gives it to the ניזק from the moment of death, the ניזק bears that loss. The מזיק pays only the difference between the live animal and the fresh carcass.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for
The drop in value of the carcass after death

steps.whatToRemember: 'והמת יהיה לו' teaches that the ניזק owns the carcass from the moment of death, so a later drop in its value is his loss.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the question is just who gets the carcass. Both sides agree it ends up with the ניזק. The real question is who bears the loss when it becomes worth less.

phrases.english: It is needed only for the drop in value of the carcass.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 28 by showing a practical difference
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Ownership of the carcass makes no difference, since the מזיק could pay with it anyway
steps.terutzMaskana: Ownership decides who bears the carcass's drop in value, and the פסוק puts that loss on the ניזק

steps.title: Is the drop in value a dispute between תנאים?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the question of פחת נבילה is already argued about by תנאים. It begins quoting a ברייתא on a פסוק about a torn animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say that the drop in value of the carcass is a dispute between תנאים? As it was taught in a ברייתא: 'If it was torn, let him bring it as a witness.'
